sources: EarthDate (Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin), Fish Out of Water: some mudskippers spend three-quarters of their lives on land; take in oxygen through skin, mouth and throat as long as they are wet; muscular pectoral fins move them across mud; eyes adapted for aerial vision and can't focus when submerged; eyes rotate independently to spot prey; blink by pulling the eyes into the head; at high tide live in burrows in the mud; burrows hold eggs and an air pocket; https://www.earthdate.org/episodes/fish-out-of-water

National Geographic magazine (2020), Mudskipper builds ideal nest for his offspring: males flare fins and leap high to court; an impressed female follows him to the burrow; eggs laid on the chamber ceiling; the male gulps air, carries it down and exhales it, roughly 100 mouthfuls to make the air bubble (Karen Martin); he times the air release so water floods in and the larvae hatch; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/mudskipper-builds-ideal-nest-for-his-offspring

BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife), Fish that can walk on land evolved the ability to blink like we do (Aiello, Stewart et al., PNAS 2023): mudskippers blink by pulling their eyeballs back into their skulls; https://discoverwildlife.com/news/fish-that-can-walk-on-land-evolved-the-ability-to-blink-like-we-do

beats.say: This fish walks out of the water, and spends most of its life on land.
The mudskipper. A fish with bulging eyes on top of its head.
It crawls across the mud on its front fins, like little arms.
It breathes through its skin and its mouth, as long as it stays wet.
And underwater, it can't even see properly. Its eyes are made for air.
Each eye swivels on its own, to spot bugs above and below.
